title: Appointed from the list, and already doing the job
question: How many permanent civil-service appointments went to someone who had already been paid in the same job class in the same department the year before, as a temporary, provisional or exempt employee?
finding: Of 22,243 permanent civil-service appointments since October 2018 that can be matched to the payroll, 3,290 (14.8%) went to someone already paid in that class in that department the fiscal year before on another footing: 1,922 as temporary exempt, 930 as permanent exempt and 438 as provisional. 325 of those 3,290 were the only person ever appointed from their eligible list, and 683 were ranked first on it. Among departments with 50 or more appointments the share is highest in Technology (50.3%), Mayor (40.8%) and Homelessness Services (36.9%). 9,005 appointments (40.5%) went to people not on the payroll the year before.
how: The Department of Human Resources’ table of permanent civil-service appointments (every appointment since 15 October 2018 except police officers, with job class, department, rank on the eligible list and the list’s number) is joined to the payroll on three things together: the employee’s name, the job class and the department, in the fiscal year of the appointment. 22,243 of 26,608 appointments match; the rest are dated after the last payroll year, belong to bodies outside the payroll file, or differ in spelling. An appointee counts as already in the job when the payroll for the fiscal year before shows the same name in the same class and department with a type of appointment other than permanent civil service. “Only appointee from the list” means no other appointment in the table cites that list. Ranked by share among departments with 50 or more matched appointments.
limits: Moving temporary staff into permanent posts is something the City does openly: the civil grand jury recorded in 2023 that the City was converting temporary workers hired at the start of the pandemic into permanent civil-service workers, and a provisional appointee is by definition waiting for the examination. Experience in the job can fairly earn a high score. The question the figure raises is narrower: where the person was chosen first and the examination followed, was the examination open to others in practice? The table gives a rank and a list number but not how many people were on the list, whether the test was written for one position, or when the job was advertised. The fiscal year before is a coarse test: someone hired as a temporary and made permanent within the same fiscal year is not counted. Human Resources’ own account of the practice, hiring as exempt pending a permanent appointment where no list existed, is quoted in the screen on the Civil Service Commission’s audits and decisions.
